stem: Which of the following is the accounting equation?

options.rationale: Correct: everything the business owns was financed by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities).
Liabilities are a source of the assets, so they belong on the same side as capital, not with the assets.
Capital is what is left for the owner after the liabilities are deducted from the assets, not added to them.
Liabilities equal assets minus capital; adding capital makes the figure far too large.

explanation: **Assets = Capital + Liabilities.** It can be rearranged as Capital = Assets − Liabilities or Liabilities = Assets − Capital.

stem: A poultry project in Chinhoyi has assets of US\$15,600 and liabilities of US\$4,350. What is the owner's capital?

options.rationale: Correct: capital = assets − liabilities.
This adds the liabilities to the assets instead of deducting them.
This is the amount owed to outsiders, not the amount owed to the owner.
This is the total of the assets; part of them was financed by liabilities.

explanation: Capital = assets − liabilities = 15,600 − 4,350 = US\$11,250.

stem: A transport operator buys a second-hand delivery van on credit from a garage in Bulawayo. What is the effect on the accounting equation?

options.rationale: The owner has not put in more money; the van has been financed by the garage.

options.content: One asset increases and another asset decreases
options.rationale: That would happen if the van were paid for by cash or bank; here nothing has been paid yet.
Correct: the van is a new asset and the amount owed to the garage is a new liability.
Buying a van adds an asset; the two sides must change in the same direction.

explanation: On credit means the business will pay later. The van (non-current asset) goes up and the amount owed to the garage (liability) goes up by the same amount.

stem: Rudo takes cash from her shop's till to pay her child's school fees. What is the effect on the accounting equation of the business?

options.rationale: The school fees are a personal cost of Rudo; the business owes nothing less to any outsider.
Correct: this is drawings. An asset (cash) and the amount owed to the owner (capital) both fall.

options.content: Cash decreases and another asset increases
options.rationale: No business asset is received in exchange; the money leaves the business.
No new debt to an outsider is created; the cash has already been taken.

explanation: Money taken by the owner for personal use is **drawings**. It reduces an asset (cash) and reduces capital. It is not a business expense.

stem: Which transaction does **not** change the total of a business's assets?

options.content: Buying goods for resale on credit from a supplier
options.rationale: Inventory rises and nothing is paid, so total assets increase.

options.content: Paying a supplier the amount owed by bank transfer
options.rationale: Bank falls while a liability falls, so total assets decrease.

options.content: The owner paying more of her savings into the business bank account
options.rationale: Bank rises and capital rises, so total assets increase.

options.content: Buying office equipment and paying by bank transfer
options.rationale: Correct: equipment goes up and bank goes down by the same amount, so total assets stay the same.

explanation: When one asset is exchanged for another (bank for equipment), one asset rises and another falls by the same amount. Total assets, liabilities and capital are unchanged.

stem: Farai sells goods that cost him US\$560 for US\$840, and the customer pays in cash. What is the effect on Farai's capital?

options.rationale: This is the cash received. Inventory costing US\$560 was also given up, so assets rose by less than this.
This is the cost of the goods given up, not the gain on the sale.
Correct: the profit on the sale belongs to the owner, so capital rises by the profit.
Selling at a profit increases net assets, so capital must rise.

explanation: Cash rises by US\$840 and inventory falls by US\$560, so assets rise by US\$280. No liability changes, so capital rises by the profit of US\$280.
hints: Look at both assets that change: cash and inventory.

stem: Sipho's capital at 1 January 2025 was US\$9,200. During 2025 he made a profit of US\$2,750 and took drawings of US\$1,400. He introduced no new capital. What was his capital at 31 December 2025?

options.rationale: Drawings have been added; they reduce capital.
This leaves out the drawings.
Profit and drawings have been treated the wrong way round.
Correct: opening capital + profit − drawings.

hints: Profit increases capital; drawings reduce it.

stem: A business's liabilities increase while its total assets stay exactly the same. What must have happened to its capital?

options.content: Capital rose by the same amount as the rise in liabilities
options.rationale: Then capital + liabilities would rise while assets stayed the same: the equation would not balance.

options.content: Capital fell by the same amount as the rise in liabilities
options.rationale: Correct: if assets are unchanged, capital + liabilities must stay the same, so capital falls.

options.content: Capital stayed the same as before
options.rationale: Capital + liabilities would then be larger than assets.

options.content: Capital rose by twice the rise in liabilities
options.rationale: Both sides must change by the same total amount, and here assets did not change at all.

explanation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. If assets do not change and liabilities rise, capital must fall by the same amount. This happens, for example, when an expense such as electricity is received on credit: it is a loss to the owner.
hints: Write the equation and keep the left-hand side fixed.

stem: Thandeka's hardware shop has assets of US\$24,000 and capital of US\$17,500. She then pays a supplier US\$1,800 by bank transfer. What are the shop's liabilities after the payment?

options.rationale: This is the figure before the payment to the supplier.
Correct: liabilities were 24,000 − 17,500 = 6,500; the payment reduces them by 1,800.
The payment reduces the amount owed; it does not add to it.
The payment does not change capital; it reduces bank (an asset) and the amount owed (a liability).

explanation: Liabilities before the payment = 24,000 − 17,500 = US\$6,500. Paying a supplier reduces bank and trade payables by US\$1,800, so liabilities become US\$4,700. Capital is unchanged at US\$17,500 and assets fall to US\$22,200.
hints: First find the liabilities before the payment.
Which two items does paying a supplier change?

stem: A school tuck shop has assets of US\$31,480 and capital of US\$22,965. Calculate its liabilities.
explanation: Liabilities = assets − capital = 31,480 − 22,965 = US\$8,515. Adding the two figures (US\$54,445) is a common slip.
workedSolution: 1. Liabilities = assets − capital = 31,480 − 22,965 = US\$8,515. Adding the two figures (US\$54,445) is a common slip.

stem: Nyasha's capital in her dressmaking business was US\$14,300 at 1 January 2025. During 2025 she paid in a further US\$2,500 of her own money, the business made a **loss** of US\$1,180, and she took drawings of US\$3,600. Calculate her capital at 31 December 2025.
explanation:
1. Closing capital = opening capital + capital introduced − loss − drawings.
2. = 14,300 + 2,500 − 1,180 − 3,600
3. = US\$12,020.

Adding the loss gives US\$14,380; leaving out the extra capital gives US\$9,520.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Closing capital = opening capital + capital introduced − loss − drawings.
2. = 14,300 + 2,500 − 1,180 − 3,600
3. = US\$12,020.

Adding the loss gives US\$14,380; leaving out the extra capital gives US\$9,520.
hints: A loss reduces capital, just as drawings do.

stem: Tatenda introduced no new capital into his welding business during 2025. His capital was US\$8,640 on 1 January 2025 and US\$11,215 on 31 December 2025. His drawings for the year were US\$2,450. Calculate the profit for the year.
explanation:
1. Closing capital = opening capital + profit − drawings, so profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings.
2. Increase in capital = 11,215 − 8,640 = 2,575.
3. Add back the drawings: 2,575 + 2,450 = US\$5,025.

The increase in capital alone (US\$2,575) understates the profit, because part of the profit was taken out as drawings.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Closing capital = opening capital + profit − drawings, so profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings.
2. Increase in capital = 11,215 − 8,640 = 2,575.
3. Add back the drawings: 2,575 + 2,450 = US\$5,025.

The increase in capital alone (US\$2,575) understates the profit, because part of the profit was taken out as drawings.
hints: Capital went up by the profit and down by the drawings.
Add the drawings back to the increase in capital.

stem: A bank loan that was used to start a business is part of the owner's capital.
explanation: False. A loan is owed to the bank, an outsider, so it is a **liability**. Capital is only what the owner has invested plus retained profit.

stem: When a business buys inventory and pays in cash, its total assets stay the same.
explanation: True. Inventory increases and cash decreases by the same amount: one asset is exchanged for another.

stem: Farai's printing business buys a computer on credit. Choose the effect on each part of the accounting equation.
explanation: The computer is a new asset and the amount owed to the supplier is a new liability. The owner has put in nothing and no profit has been made, so capital does not change.

stem: A customer of Chipo's wholesale shop pays the amount she owes by bank transfer. Choose the effect on each total.
explanation: Bank increases and trade receivables (also an asset) decrease by the same amount. Total assets do not change, and neither liabilities nor capital are affected. The sale itself, and its profit, were recorded when the goods were sold.
hints: Money owed by a customer is an asset of the business.
Two assets change: one up, one down.

stem: Match each transaction with its effect on the accounting equation.

left.content: The owner pays more of her own money into the business bank account
Goods for resale are bought on credit
A supplier is paid by bank transfer
Office furniture is bought for cash
The owner takes goods from the shop for her family

right.content: An asset and a liability both decrease
One asset increases and another decreases
An asset and capital both decrease
An asset and capital both increase
An asset and a liability both increase

explanation: Each transaction changes two items. Capital changes only for the owner's dealings (capital introduced, drawings) and for profits or losses.

stem: Explain why the accounting equation always balances.

points.description: Every asset of the business has been provided either by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities), so the two sides measure the same resources.
Every transaction has two effects (dual aspect) of equal amount, so after each transaction both sides still agree.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The assets are the resources of the business, and capital plus liabilities show where those resources came from, so the totals must be the same. Each transaction has two equal effects, for example buying goods on credit increases inventory and trade payables by the same amount, so the equation stays in balance.

explanation: Two ideas earn the marks: the two sides describe the same resources (what the business has and who provided it), and the dual aspect of every transaction keeps them equal.

stem:
Tatenda started a phone repair business in Gweru on 1 June 2025. His transactions for June were:

| Date | Transaction |
| --- | --- |
| 1 June | Tatenda pays US\$4,500 of his own money into a business bank account. |
| 4 June | Buys repair tools and equipment for US\$1,350, paying by bank transfer. |
| 9 June | Buys spare parts (inventory) for US\$980 on credit from Chipo Electronics. |
| 15 June | Completes repairs for customers using spare parts that cost US\$210. The customers pay US\$620 into the bank. |
| 20 June | Pays Chipo Electronics US\$600 by bank transfer. |
| 27 June | Takes US\$250 from the business bank account for personal use. |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the balance of the business bank account at 30 June 2025.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the value of the inventory of spare parts at 30 June 2025.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total assets of the business at 30 June 2025.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit made in June 2025.
parts.explanation: Repair income 620 − spare parts used 210 = US\$410.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Repair income 620 − spare parts used 210 = US\$410.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the payment of US\$600 to Chipo Electronics on 20 June did not change Tatenda's capital.

points.description: The payment reduced an asset (bank) by US\$600.
It reduced a liability (trade payables) by the same amount, so assets − liabilities, and therefore capital, did not change (no profit or loss arises).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Bank fell by US\$600 and the amount owed to Chipo Electronics fell by US\$600. Net assets stayed the same, so capital was unchanged.

explanation: At 30 June: bank US\$2,920, equipment US\$1,350, inventory US\$770 (total assets US\$5,040); trade payables US\$380; capital US\$4,660. Check: 380 + 4,660 = 5,040.
hints: Work through the transactions in order, changing two items each time.
The profit on 15 June is the repair income less the cost of the parts used.

parts.label: (c)
parts.explanation: Opening capital = closing capital − profit + drawings = 6,040 − 3,420 + 1,900 = US\$4,520.
